scams.name: Adelaide Taxi Short-Run Overcharge
scams.tldr: Adelaide airport taxi drivers add undisclosed fuel surcharges, late-night rates, and phantom "airport fees" to a metered fare, presenting tourists with bills of $65–$99 for the 7-km CBD run from Adelaide Airport — a pattern extensively documented on traveler forums.
scams.description:
Adelaide Airport is 7 km from the hotel strip on North Terrace — a ride that Uber quotes at $25–$35 and that a correctly metered taxi should cost a similar amount. The problem is not the meter itself but the additions: a fuel surcharge not posted inside the cab, a late-night rate applied outside its legal window, and an "airport fee" that has no regulatory basis. Tourists unfamiliar with South Australian taxi regulations have no immediate way to know which charges are legal and which are invented.

The meter can also be tampered to click in $0.40 increments rather than the legal $0.35 or smaller. By the time the discrepancy is visible, the trip is over and the driver has created time pressure to pay and leave. Documented Adelaide cases include a $99 bill for a 15-minute ride — more than three times what the distance justifies at any legal rate.

The safest option is to bypass the taxi rank entirely. Use Uber or DiDi from the Adelaide Airport rideshare bay for a typical CBD fare of $25–$40, or take the JetExpress bus (J1, J2, J3, J7, or J8) to the CBD for $5.40 with a Metrocard. If you must take a taxi, photograph the plate and driver ID before the trip, watch the meter for $0.40 increments, and pay by card on the in-car terminal. Disputed charges can be reported to the South Australian Public Transport Authority at adelaidemetro.com.au.
scams.location: Adelaide Airport taxi rank, CBD (King William, Rundle Mall), North Terrace hotel ranks

scams.name: DiDi / Uber 'Cancel Mid-Trip' Charge Scam
scams.tldr: DiDi drivers in Adelaide's CBD accept a ride booking, move the car 100 meters down the road, end the trip in the app while the passenger is still waiting at the pickup point, and collect a $15 cancellation fee plus part-trip fare — a phantom-pickup exploit that abuses the app's driver-compensation structure.
scams.description:
Rideshare apps compensate drivers for genuine trip interruptions through cancellation fees and part-trip fares — a legitimate mechanism that protects drivers from no-shows. Some Adelaide DiDi drivers exploit this by accepting a booking, moving the vehicle a short distance to register a "pickup," then ending the trip in the app before the passenger has entered the car. A related variant involves the driver claiming an "app issue" and insisting on direct cash payment — bypassing the platform's refund and dispute mechanisms entirely.

The passenger waiting at the pickup point sees the trip end on their phone. Their card is charged $15 for a cancellation fee and a partial trip fare. The driver moves on to repeat the process. Adelaide traveler reports identify DiDi CBD drivers as the predominant offender in this pattern; the scam volume is highest during event nights around Rundle Mall and the Adelaide Oval.

The platform's dispute system is the primary recourse, but it requires documentation taken immediately. If a driver ends a trip before you are in the vehicle, screenshot the ride details in the app right away, then request a refund in-app citing the trip-end discrepancy — if the platform stalls beyond 72 hours, escalate to a credit card chargeback. Switching to Uber for short CBD trips is a practical workaround for the DiDi phantom-pickup pattern, despite Uber's own separate taxi-overcharge risk at the airport.
scams.location: CBD DiDi and Uber pickups, Rundle Mall, Adelaide Oval precinct

scams.name: Fake Barossa / McLaren Vale Wine Tour Booking
scams.tldr: Fake wine tour operators targeting Adelaide-based searches for Barossa and McLaren Vale day trips collect $79–$150 upfront via bank transfer — the key scam tell — then go silent before departure day, leaving no record, no refund, and no tour.
scams.description:
The Barossa Valley and McLaren Vale are South Australia's most popular tourist destinations, making "Adelaide wine tour" a high-value search term for both legitimate operators and scammers. Fraudulent booking sites use Google Ads to appear above established operators, offering full-day tours with hotel pickup, four wineries, and lunch included at prices ($79–$150) that signal great value but are below what a legitimate operator can deliver while remaining viable.

The tell is the payment method. Legitimate tour operators accept credit card payment with a booking confirmation sent to your email. Fake sites request bank transfer to "avoid card fees," sometimes framed as a temporary "technical issue" with the card terminal. Payment by bank transfer is nearly impossible to recover; the scammer's account is typically emptied within hours of receiving funds. Some operations use cloned sites that mimic legitimate Barossa operators closely enough that the difference is invisible without checking the business's ABN.

Bank transfer to an unknown operator is the definitive warning sign for this category. Book wine tours only with operators who have a verifiable Australian Business Number (searchable at abn.business.gov.au), a physical Adelaide office, and credit card payment — established operators include Groovy Grape Tours (groovygrape.com.au), Taste the Barossa (tastethebarossa.com.au), and Barossa Daimler (barossadaimler.com.au). Pay by credit card exclusively: it is the only payment method that allows a chargeback if the operator fails to deliver.
scams.location: Online booking (Google Ads spoofed results), Facebook wine-tour groups

scams.name: Adelaide Fake Rental / Facebook Airbnb Invoice Scam
scams.tldr: A scammer advertising a North Adelaide short-stay on Facebook Marketplace sends a convincingly branded "Airbnb invoice" PDF and requests a bank transfer of $840 — an accommodation fraud that exploits Airbnb's visual identity while operating entirely outside the platform.
scams.description:
Adelaide's short-term rental market drives tourists and short-stay seekers to Facebook Marketplace, where prices look competitive and the listings appear personal and legitimate. Scammers post plausible properties — a one-bedroom in North Adelaide at $120/night — and when contacted, provide detailed communication that mimics an authentic Airbnb host experience, including a PDF with accurate Airbnb branding, a booking reference number, and a request to bank transfer the total amount to "confirm the reservation."

When the money is transferred, communication stops. Airbnb has no record of the booking because the booking was never made through Airbnb. The PDF invoice was created to look like a legitimate confirmation. Traveler reports confirm Adelaide is a recurring target in this pattern, with scammers cycling through new Facebook Marketplace accounts after each successful fraud.

Airbnb does not invoice guests via PDF and does not request bank transfers. Any "Airbnb invoice" received outside the official Airbnb app that asks for a bank transfer is a scam — legitimate Airbnb bookings are confirmed only inside the Airbnb app with payment processed by Airbnb directly. For short stays, always book through the Airbnb app using a bookmarked URL rather than following a link sent in a message. If you have already transferred funds, call your bank within 24 hours and request a payment recall before the scammer moves the money.
scams.location: Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree, and fake email links posing as Airbnb

scams.name: International Student Visa / Education Agent Fraud
scams.tldr: Migration agents advertising on social media in Adelaide charge international students $8,000–$13,000 for visa pathways and PR sponsorship via unaccredited colleges — a fraud targeting prospective students unfamiliar with Australia's registered agent and CRICOS course verification systems.
scams.description:
Adelaide has a significant international student population, and a parallel ecosystem of unregistered migration agents has emerged to target prospective students unfamiliar with Australian visa pathways. These agents advertise on Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp groups in the languages of the communities they target. They offer "guaranteed PR sponsorship" through an Adelaide-based college and charge upfront fees of $8,000–$13,000, typically in cash.

The pathway does not exist as described. The college may be real but unaccredited for immigration purposes, or entirely fictitious. The visa application may be lodged defectively or never lodged at all. Students discover the problem when their course enrolment is rejected, their visa application is denied, or the agent stops responding. Adelaide's lower-cost international education market has attracted a disproportionate concentration of these schemes compared to Sydney and Melbourne.

Australia maintains public registers that make agent and institution verification straightforward. Only engage MARA-registered migration agents — verify any agent's registration at the mara.gov.au public register before paying anything — and only enrol in CRICOS-registered institutions, searchable at cricos.education.gov.au. Never pay cash for visa or education services; always pay by card or bank transfer to a registered ABN with a receipt. Any promise of "guaranteed PR" is fraudulent — no legitimate agent can guarantee a visa outcome.
scams.location: Social media (Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram), migration-agent offices across Adelaide

scams.name: Fake 'SA Tourism Voucher' / Booking Voucher Scam
scams.tldr: Phishing emails and SMS claiming to offer South Australian Tourism Commission vouchers ($100–$200 off hotel stays) direct recipients to cloned government-branded sites that harvest credit card details — an identity-theft operation that exploits the credibility of genuine past SA government voucher programs.
scams.description:
The South Australian government ran legitimate tourism voucher programs during the 2020–2022 tourism recovery period, and that credibility is what scammers exploit. Phishing campaigns send emails or SMS claiming to offer "$100 off any SA hotel stay this winter" or "Cost is Calling Voucher — claim yours before Friday." The branding closely matches the South Australian Tourism Commission's visual identity, including the logo, color palette, and domain-adjacent email addresses.

The link leads to a site that mimics southaustralia.com in design. To "verify the voucher," the site asks for personal details and card information for a small "processing fee" or "identity check." Once entered, the card is tested with small charges ($1–$3) that appear legitimate, then used for larger unauthorized transactions. The voucher never arrives. Local reports consistently identify the pattern and confirm the sites are not affiliated with the SA government.

Any genuine South Australian government voucher program is announced only on official .gov.au domains, never by unsolicited email or SMS. Never click a voucher link in an email or SMS — go directly to southaustralia.com or tourism.sa.gov.au and check the promotions section to verify whether any offer exists before entering personal information or card details. For genuine SA tourism discounts, use established booking platforms such as Booking.com, Stayz, or Wotif. Report phishing attempts to ScamWatch at scamwatch.gov.au.
scams.location: Phishing emails and SMS targeting SA residents and visitors
